title: Pediatric GI, Part 1: Nutrition and acute abdomen

sections.title: Calories and infant formula
notes: Carbohydrate and protein **4 kcal/g**, fat **9 kcal/g**.
Formula: **20 kcal per 30 mL (1 oz)**. Term and preterm need **100 to 140 kcal/kg/day**, malnourished kids 20 to 30% more for catch-up.
Protein: preterm **3.5 g/kg/day**, term 2 to 2.5 g/kg/day.

sections.title: Breast milk and breastfeeding contraindications
notes: Breast milk: carbohydrate **lactose**, protein alpha-lactalbumin, fat ARA and DHA.
Absolute contraindications: **HIV** (even on treatment), **HTLV**, **active untreated TB** (fine after 2 weeks of treatment), infant **classic galactosemia**.
Fine to breastfeed: **hepatitis B or C**, maternal fever, mastitis or breast abscess, smoking (counsel to quit), infant jaundice (feed more often).

sections.title: Preterm formula
notes: Carbohydrate: corn syrup solids (glucose polymers). Whey to casein 60:40, like human milk. Fat: **medium-chain triglycerides**.
**Calcium to phosphorus 2:1** for best calcium absorption (matters for preterm TPN). Zinc high, over 10 times copper.

sections.title: Marasmus vs kwashiorkor
notes: **Marasmus**: non-edematous, severe energy and protein lack. Severe wasting, hypotonia, wrinkled old-man face, listless, low temperature, slow pulse.
**Kwashiorkor**: edematous, **protein lack with adequate carbohydrate**. Low albumin causes **edema** and puffy face. Low lipoprotein synthesis causes **fatty liver**, so the big belly is liver.
Kwashiorkor: infections (no antibodies), apathy, irritability, **flaky mosaic skin** (low zinc, looks like acrodermatitis enteropathica), sparse **red or grey streaky hair**.

sections.title: Thiamine (B1) and riboflavin (B2)
notes: B1 deficiency causes: TPN without thiamine, **chronic alcohol use**. Infantile beriberi: **heart failure**, hoarseness or aphonia, absent reflexes. Adults: **Wernicke** (confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia, nystagmus). Give IV thiamine to alcohol users in the ED.

B2 deficiency: **prolonged phototherapy** (destroys riboflavin), adolescent girls, low income. Signs: **angular stomatitis and cheilitis, glossitis**, keratitis, photophobia, **seborrheic dermatitis**, anemia.

sections.title: Niacin (B3) and pyridoxine (B6)
notes: B3: alcohol, **prolonged isoniazid**, malabsorption, anorexia. **3 Ds: diarrhea, dermatitis, dementia**.
B6: **isoniazid** (supplement B6 on TB treatment), breastfed over 6 months by a deficient mother.

**Pyridoxine-dependent seizures**: intractable seizures under 18 months, can start in utero. Any persistent seizure with no clear cause gets a **trial of pyridoxine**. B6 deficiency also gives microcytic anemia, neuropathy, dermatitis.

sections.title: B12 deficiency
notes: Case: 1-year-old, **strict vegan mother**, pale, macrocytic anemia.
B12 comes **only from animal foods**. Causes: vegan diet, **ileal resection or Crohn of the ileum**, pernicious anemia, exclusive breastfeeding by a deficient mother.

Picture: **megaloblastic anemia, hypersegmented neutrophils**, paresthesias, **posterior column loss (vibration)**, hyperpigmentation, failure to thrive. Low maternal B12 in pregnancy: neural tube defects. Treat the cause, then B12.

sections.title: Folate deficiency
notes: Case: 6-month-old on **homemade goat's milk formula**, macrocytic anemia. **Goat's milk lacks folate**.
Causes: goat's milk, Crohn, sickle cell, malignancy, **phenytoin, methotrexate**, MTHFR deficiency.
Macrocytic anemia: check **serum folate and B12**. Never treat B12 deficiency with folate alone, neuro signs get worse.

sections.title: Vitamin C deficiency (scurvy)
notes: Case: 7-month-old on **evaporated boiled milk**, **bleeding gums**, won't move legs, **frog-leg position**.
Signs: gingivitis and bleeding gums, perifollicular hemorrhage, **leg pain from subperiosteal hemorrhage**, hemarthrosis, pseudoparalysis, poor wound healing.
Too much vitamin C: **kidney stones**, diarrhea, hemolysis in G6PD.

sections.title: Fat-soluble vitamins and vitamin A
notes: **A, D, E, K** need bowel surface and enzymes: low in **short bowel, cystic fibrosis, celiac, cholestasis**.
Vitamin A deficiency: first sign **night blindness**, then xerophthalmia, **Bitot spots**, corneal ulcer, **keratomalacia** (emergency, IV vitamin A). Follicular hyperkeratosis.
**Measles: give vitamin A** (deficiency raises mortality).
Too much vitamin A: **idiopathic intracranial hypertension** (headache, papilledema, normal CT, high opening pressure), hepatosplenomegaly, alopecia.

sections.title: Vitamin D deficiency
notes: Case: 16-month-old, **exclusively breastfed with no supplement**, no teeth, **rachitic rosary**, wide wrists, bowed legs.
All breastfed babies need **vitamin D from birth**. Signs: poor growth, tetany from low calcium, weakness, bone deformities, **delayed teeth**.
Too much vitamin D: **hypercalcemia**, constipation, nephrocalcinosis, kidney stones.

sections.title: Vitamin E deficiency
notes: Case: ex-24-weeker with **cholestatic jaundice** awaiting transplant, **hyporeflexia**, weakness, low alpha-tocopherol.
Causes: **biliary atresia**, very low birth weight preterms, **cystic fibrosis**, malabsorption.
Signs: **areflexia, ataxia, loss of position and vibration sense**, ophthalmoplegia, **hemolytic anemia in preterms**.

sections.title: Vitamin K deficiency bleeding
notes: Case: 5-day-old **born at home**, bleeding from the umbilical stump: **no vitamin K at birth**.
Vitamin K makes **factors 2, 7, 9, 10**. Breast milk is low in it, it doesn't cross the placenta, and the newborn gut has no flora yet.
Diagnosis: **prolonged PT**. Prevention: **0.5 to 1 mg IM at birth**. Treat with vitamin K, then fresh frozen plasma.

sections.title: Iron deficiency anemia
notes: Peak at 6 to 20 months, especially exclusively breastfed. Iron supplement from **4 months for term, from birth for preterm** (US guidance).
Picture: poor school work, irritability, glossitis, angular cheilitis, **pica and pagophagia (ice)**, more lead absorption, **lower IQ**.

sections.title: Zinc, copper, selenium, biotin, iodine
notes: Zinc: alopecia, diarrhea, dermatitis, infections, poor growth, loss of taste. **Acrodermatitis enteropathica**: autosomal recessive, starts **after weaning**, scaly rash around the **mouth and anus**, alopecia, diarrhea.
Copper: microcytic anemia, **neutropenia**, metaphyseal flaring like rickets with normal vitamin D. **Menkes**: X-linked, **kinky colourless hair**, seizures, hypotonia, low copper and ceruloplasmin.
Selenium: **cardiomyopathy**. Biotin: alopecia, dermatitis, hypotonia. Iodine: goitre, **cretinism**.

sections.title: Carotenemia and refeeding syndrome
notes: **Carotenemia**: yellow skin (nose), **white sclera**, lots of carrots. Reassure.

**Refeeding syndrome**: full calories too fast in severe malnutrition (anorexia). Insulin drives **phosphate, magnesium and potassium** into cells: **severe hypophosphatemia**, ATP depletion, organ failure, death.

sections.title: Failure to thrive
notes: Weight under the 3rd to 5th percentile for length, **dropping 2 major percentile lines**, or under 80% of ideal weight. Plot weight, length and head circumference.

Causes to think of: reflux, **malrotation with intermittent volvulus**, raised intracranial pressure, **celiac (after 6 months)**, abuse, cow's milk protein allergy, heart failure, **renal tubular acidosis, UTI**, hyperthyroidism, Russell-Silver.
**Weight falls before height**: GI or nutritional cause (cystic fibrosis, celiac).

sections.title: Failure to thrive workup and management
notes: Labs: CBC, chemistry (acidosis, RTA, kidney and liver), **anti-tTG IgA (with IgA level)**, stool fat and reducing substances, **sweat chloride even without lung symptoms**, TSH and T4, urinalysis.
Admit if: severe malnutrition, unstable, outpatient care failing, **abuse or neglect**, poor parent-child interaction.
Management: **multidisciplinary**, watch a feed, more and better calories, OT and speech for food aversion, treat the cause.

sections.title: Acute abdominal pain: causes
notes: Sudden pain with **bilious vomiting and distension: midgut volvulus**. Colicky pain and lethargy at about 9 months: intussusception.
Always think of **ovarian torsion** in girls and **testicular torsion** in boys (hours to save it).
Trauma: spleen or liver rupture, **duodenal hematoma (bike handlebar)**, abuse. Right lower lobe pneumonia can present as abdominal pain.
Teen girls: **pregnancy test**, PID, Fitz-Hugh-Curtis, ectopic. Also constipation, gastroenteritis, mesenteric adenitis, UTI.

sections.title: Appendicitis: diagnosis
notes: Missed most often in **young children**, who perforate most. Anorexia and fever can be absent.
Pain worse with **walking or movement**, progressive. **Localized tenderness is the single most reliable finding**, repeat the exam. Use gentle percussion, not deep palpation.
Look-alikes: **mesenteric adenitis** (gets better, enlarged nodes, normal appendix, Yersinia from raw pork), **right lower lobe pneumonia** (chest x-ray).

sections.title: Appendicitis: signs, labs and imaging
notes: Rovsing (left lower quadrant pressure hurts right), obturator (internal rotation of flexed hip), psoas (hip extension). Dunphy (cough), Markle (heel drop).
CBC can be normal in the first 24 hours. WBC over 20,000 suggests perforation. Urine can have WBCs but **no bacteria**.
**Ultrasound first**: wall over **6 mm**, non-compressible. Must see a normal appendix to rule it out. CT is the gold standard but avoid if possible.

sections.title: Appendicitis: management
notes: Classic case on the exam: **straight to surgery**, no more tests.
**Morphine does not reduce diagnostic accuracy**, treat the pain.
Antibiotics: one preop dose. Perforated: 3 to 5 days (ampicillin, gentamicin plus clindamycin or metronidazole, or ceftriaxone plus metronidazole).

sections.title: Midgut volvulus
notes: **Surgical emergency** with persistent bilious vomiting. Malrotation lets bowel twist and cut off its blood supply: necrosis, short bowel, death.
Usually **under 1 year**, can be any age. Bilious vomiting can be absent if the twist is above the ampulla.
Older kids: pain. Infants: lethargy, poor feeding, crying. **Rectal bleeding is late** (ischemia).
Upper GI contrast is the main test: **corkscrew** duodenum or abrupt cutoff. Plain film: dilated stomach and proximal duodenum. Call surgery **before any test**.

sections.title: Intussusception
notes: **Most common cause of intestinal obstruction** in infants. Usually ileocolic.
Lead points explain older kids: **Meckel**, polyps, **lymphoma**, duplication cyst, HSP. Infants: idiopathic, enlarged nodes after a virus.
Intermittent colicky pain (constant pain points to appendicitis), **lethargy out of proportion**, may be the only sign. Vomiting can be absent or bilious.
**Currant jelly stool is late**, a non-bloody stool doesn't rule it out. Sausage mass in the **right upper quadrant**, empty right lower quadrant.

sections.title: Intussusception: imaging and recurrence
notes: Ultrasound: **target or donut sign**, very sensitive and specific.
**Air contrast enema is diagnostic and therapeutic**. On the board, pick air enema over ultrasound for a classic case.
Recurrence about **10%**, most within **72 hours**. Repeat the enema. More than one recurrence suggests a **lead point**.

sections.title: Ileus
notes: Poor motility without obstruction: pain, distension, vomiting, **hypoactive bowel sounds**.
Causes: surgery, infection and sepsis, **hypokalemia**, narcotics, anesthetics, chemo.
Supportive: stop feeds, IV fluids, NG tube only if vomiting or distended, treat the cause.

sections.title: Acute pancreatitis
notes: Most common cause in kids: **blunt abdominal trauma** (handlebar, abuse). Also biliary anomalies, drugs (**valproate, L-asparaginase, steroids, tetracycline, azathioprine**), viruses, **high triglycerides, hypercalcemia**, cystic fibrosis. 25% unknown.
Pain often does **not radiate to the back** in kids. Pseudocyst: epigastric mass.
**Amylase and lipase 3 times normal**, lipase more specific. Normal levels don't rule it out. First imaging: **ultrasound**. CT if tumour suspected.
Treatment: NPO (can eat if no pain), IV fluids, analgesia (narcotics for severe pain), acid suppression, NG if vomiting. Pseudocyst under 5 cm: watch 4 to 6 weeks.

sections.title: Recurrent pancreatitis
notes: Causes: **hypertriglyceridemia**, hypercalcemia, **hereditary pancreatitis** (most common cause of relapsing pancreatitis in the US).
Risks: pancreatic insufficiency, adenocarcinoma, pseudocyst.
Case: recurrent pain, family history of **early cardiac death**, high lipase: **hyperlipidemia**.

sections.title: Acute cholecystitis and gallstones
notes: Causes: **gallstones**, hemolysis (**sickle cell, G6PD**), TPN, **ceftriaxone**, ileal resection, cystic fibrosis. Acalculous: critical illness and sepsis.
Right upper quadrant pain, **Murphy sign**, fever, vomiting, jaundice.
Cholesterol stones are radiolucent. **Pigment stones are black, radiopaque, from hemolysis**. Ultrasound first, HIDA if not seen.
Treatment: NPO, IV fluids, pain control, antibiotics if febrile or sick, cholecystectomy timing with surgery.

sections.title: Choledocholithiasis and cholangitis
notes: Stone in the common bile duct: obstructive jaundice, high direct bilirubin, GGT and alkaline phosphatase.
Cholangitis: infection behind the stone (fever, jaundice, right upper quadrant pain). Needs antibiotics and duct drainage.
